Responses are normalized to a one-percentage-point increase in the contribution rate to private pension pillars. The specification includes one lag of the dependent variable, contemporaneous values, and three lags of the old-age dependency ratio, the unemployment rate, the age (first) factor, and a crisis dummy, along with horizon-specific country and year fixed effects. Inferences based on bootstrapped standard errors (1000 replications). Wald test statistics for joint significance and p-values are reported below each chart. Darker (lighter) shaded areas indicate 68% (95%) pointwise confidence intervals.

Labour market outcomes. As shown in Figure 12, the labour-market effects of the Capitalisation factor differ markedly from those associated with retirement-age reforms. The LFPR of older workers shows no significant response (panel a), consistent with Testable Implication 2, which anticipated a weak and ambiguous effect of financing-structure reforms on retirement timing. Similarly, the aggregate participation rate is essentially unaffected (panel b). The unemployment rate, however, rises in a non-negligible manner in the short run (panel c). The response averages +0.37 pp over the estimation window, reaches a peak of +0.80 pp at horizon 3, and then gradually fades. This increase was not explicitly predicted for the Capitalisation reform, which was expected to have limited direct labour-market effects. A plausible interpretation is that the transition toward funded private accounts generates uncertainty and short-run adjustment costs, while the associated demand contraction may temporarily weaken labour demand. This can raise unemployment even if the reform has no direct effect on statutory retirement incentives. This interpretation is consistent with the broader uncertainty channel emphasised by Bi & Zubairy (2023), although their mechanism was originally developed in the context of retirement-age reforms with long implementation lags. Overall, the labour-market results provide suggestive evidence that the Capitalisation factor has limited effects on participation, while potentially generating temporary unemployment through demand-compression and adjustment channels.

Notes: The dependent variable is the cumulative change in labour market outcomes—relative to t{-}1. Responses are normalized to a one-percentage-point increase in the contribution rate to private pension pillars. The specification includes one lag of the dependent variable, contemporaneous values, and three lags of the old-age dependency ratio, the unemployment rate, the age (first) factor, and a crisis dummy, along with horizon-specific country and year fixed effects. For the unemployment-rate regressions, the unemployment rate is excluded from the set of controls. Inferences based on bootstrapped standard errors (1000 replications). Wald test statistics for joint significance and p-values are reported below each chart. Darker (lighter) shaded areas indicate 68% (95%) pointwise confidence intervals.

Consumption and savings. Figure 13 shows that the Capitalisation factor is associated with a markedly different consumption pattern from that observed for retirement-age reforms. Private consumption falls significantly in absolute terms across the entire ten-year window (panel a, average −0.05%, significant throughout), with no sign of recovery. As a share of GDP, however, consumption is positive up to horizon 3–4 before reverting toward zero (panel b, average +0.26 pp). This apparently paradoxical combination — consumption falling in levels but rising as a share of GDP — reflects the fact that the Capitalisation reform compresses GDP proportionally more than it compresses consumption (as documented previously in the paragraph “GDP and productive capacity”), raising the consumption share mechanically. This pattern is consistent with a current-demand compression channel: the redirection of contributions toward private funded accounts may reduce consumption in levels, while the associated GDP contraction mechanically raises the consumption-to-GDP ratio.

Notes: The dependent variable is the cumulative change in consumption—relative to t{-}1. Responses are normalized to a one-percentage-point increase in the contribution rate to private pension pillars. The specification includes one lag of the dependent variable, contemporaneous values, and three lags of the old-age dependency ratio, the unemployment rate, the age (first) factor, and a crisis dummy, along with horizon-specific country and year fixed effects. Inferences based on bootstrapped standard errors (1000 replications). Wald test statistics for joint significance and p-values are reported below each chart. Darker (lighter) shaded areas indicate 68% (95%) pointwise confidence intervals.

Figure 14 reports the corresponding savings responses. For the Capitalisation factor, the savings picture is contrasted. In levels, gross domestic savings fall significantly throughout the window (panel b, average −0.06%), mirroring the GDP contraction documented above in the paragraph on GDP and productive capacity: lower output mechanically reduces aggregate savings in levels. As a share of GDP, gross domestic savings also decline over horizons 0–4 before reverting toward zero (panel a, average −0.34 pp). Gross savings in levels display a similar pattern (panel d, average −0.06%), while gross savings as a share of GDP are not jointly significant (panel c). Taken together, these results suggest that the Capitalisation factor is not associated with an increase in aggregate saving rates. A standard argument in favour of funded pension schemes holds that mandatory private pension contributions should raise saving and, eventually, investment. Our results are instead consistent with a demand-compression mechanism: higher contributions may increase saving at the household level, but the associated contraction in aggregate demand and output may compress household incomes broadly, offsetting the saving gains of contributors and preventing any increase in aggregate saving at the macroeconomic level. This interpretation remains suggestive, however, since our aggregate saving measures do not separately identify mandatory private pension contributions from other forms of saving.

Notes: The dependent variable is the cumulative change in savings—relative to t{-}1. Responses are normalized to a one-percentage-point increase in the contribution rate to private pension pillars. The specification includes one lag of the dependent variable, contemporaneous values, and three lags of the old-age dependency ratio, the unemployment rate, the age (first) factor, and a crisis dummy, along with horizon-specific country and year fixed effects. Inferences based on bootstrapped standard errors (1000 replications). Wald test statistics for joint significance and p-values are reported below each chart. Darker (lighter) shaded areas indicate 68% (95%) pointwise confidence intervals.

Investment. The Capitalisation factor is associated with a long-lasting negative investment response (Figure 15) — a result that contrasts with the theoretical prediction of a positive capital market channel. In levels (panel a), investment falls throughout the window, with an average of −0.06%, significant on most horizons. As a share of GDP (panel b), the response is negative and significant over horizons 0–7, before reverting toward zero, with an average of −0.42 pp. Fixed investment mirrors this pattern (panels c–d): average −0.06% in levels and −0.23 pp as a share of GDP, with a trough around h=4–5 before partial recovery. Testable Implication 6 had left open the possibility of a neutral or negative short-run response if demand contracted before the fiscal consolidation channel took hold. However, the standard prediction — that private pension contributions flow into capital markets and stimulate investment over the medium-to-long run — does not materialise within our estimation window. Instead, the demand contraction associated with the Capitalisation factor appears to dominate, depressing investment through a standard accelerator mechanism. Whether the capital market channel eventually prevails beyond the ten-year horizon covered here remains an open question, but within this window the Capitalisation factor is associated with persistently negative investment responses.

Darker (lighter) shaded areas indicate 68% (95%) pointwise confidence intervals.

Government debt and fiscal space. Figure 16 reveals a consistent pattern for the Capitalisation reform: expenditure falls in levels but expenditure ratios do not. In constant USD, public pension expenditure declines significantly throughout the window (panel b, average −0.04%), and central and general government expenditure follow the same pattern (panels d and f, average −0.03%). As shares of GDP, however, none of these series decline: the pension-to-GDP ratio is essentially unchanged (panel a, not jointly significant), while central and general government expenditure ratios actually rise (panels c and e, average +0.54 pp and +0.71 pp). This apparent paradox reflects the sharp GDP contraction documented above: as the denominator shrinks, expenditure ratios rise mechanically even as spending falls in levels.

Darker (lighter) shaded areas indicate 68% (95%) pointwise confidence intervals.

Government debt presents a contrasting picture (Figure 17): both central government debt (panel a, average +2.42 pp of GDP) and general government debt (panel b, average +3.72 pp of GDP) increase and are statistically different from zero at the 68% confidence level. This pattern is consistent with the transition-cost channel associated with pension privatization: as contributions are redirected toward private accounts, governments may need to continue financing existing pay-as-you-go obligations while part of the contribution base is shifted away from the public system, generating additional borrowing needs in the short to medium run. In constant USD, general and central government debts are not statistically significant (panels c–d), suggesting that the increase in debt ratios partly reflects the adverse denominator effect of the GDP contraction previously documented.

Darker (lighter) shaded areas indicate 68% (95%) pointwise confidence intervals.

External sector. As shown in Figure 18 and Figure 19, the Capitalisation factor is associated with a different external-sector profile. Export and import volumes decline over the estimation window (Figure 18, panels a and c, average -0.03% and -0.04%, respectively), mirroring the GDP contraction previously documented. As aggregate activity contracts, both export supply and import demand fall in level terms, while their shares of GDP remain broadly stable (panels b and d). Importantly, neither the trade balance nor the current account balance improves significantly (Figure 19, panels a–b). This contrasts with the theoretical possibility described in Testable Implication 8: funded pension reforms could improve the current account if they raised national saving relative to investment. The results suggest that this saving-investment channel does not materialise within the ten-year horizon. A plausible explanation is that the saving rate does not rise, as previously documented, so the mechanism through which the current account could improve is absent.

Productivity. The Capitalisation factor, by contrast, is associated with a negative response in both productivity indicators (Figure 20). TFP declines from impact, reaches a trough around horizons 1–3, and gradually reverts toward zero by horizons 4–5, leaving the average response close to zero over the full window (panel a). GDP per worker exhibits a more severe and persistent contraction, averaging −0.06% and remaining significantly below zero across most of the ten-year window (panel b). These results partly diverge from Testable Implication 9, which allowed for a negative short-run effect and a positive longer-run effect if funded pension savings translated into capital deepening. A plausible interpretation is that the demand contraction associated with the Capitalisation factor depresses output and investment while labour input adjusts only gradually. This mechanically lowers GDP per worker and may also weigh on measured TFP through lower capacity utilization or weaker investment in productivity-enhancing capital. The persistence of the negative GDP-per-worker response suggests that the capital-accumulation channel does not materialise within the ten-year horizon of our analysis.

6.2 Saving outflows and capitalisation reforms

Results in Section 6.1 point to an overall contractionary pattern associated with the Capitalisation factor, operating through both supply and demand. We now provide suggestive evidence on a possible channel underlying these results. Figure 21 and Figure 22 report, respectively, the responses of GDP (real and potential) and investment (in real terms and as a share of GDP) for two subsamples split at the median of the ratio of foreign assets to gross domestic savings. Foreign assets are defined as the sum of the stocks of portfolio equity assets, portfolio debt assets, other investment assets, and FDI assets.7 This indicator provides a proxy for the extent to which domestic savings are invested abroad rather than in the domestic economy.

7 Data are from Lane & Milesi-Ferretti (2018).

The depressing effects are concentrated exclusively in observations above the median. Real GDP decreases significantly over the entire horizon, by 0.06% on average, and most of this contraction stems from potential GDP, which shrinks by 0.05% on average. This erosion of potential output is consistent with the negative response of investment, both in real terms (-0.08% on average) and as a share of GDP (-0.78 pp on average for total investment and -0.64 pp for fixed investment). Conversely, no significant effect emerges, for either GDP or investment, in observations below the median. Overall, these results show that the negative responses associated with the Capitalisation factor are concentrated in observations with higher foreign asset holdings relative to domestic savings. This pattern is consistent with the hypothesis that the domestic benefits of higher pension savings are weaker when a larger share of savings is invested abroad.

6.3 Robustness checks

This section presents robustness analyses aimed at strengthening the causal interpretation of our findings along four dimensions: falsification (placebo) tests, controls for concurrent fiscal adjustments, spillovers and external pressures, and uncertainty. Each addresses a distinct identification threat: spurious relationships, omitted-variable bias from concurrent fiscal consolidations, contamination through spillovers or external pressures, and the possibility that economic uncertainty — domestic or foreign — surrounding the reforms may itself affect the outcomes of interest.

Falsification tests. Are our results merely artefacts, or could they arise by chance? We investigate this question through a falsification exercise. More specifically, we conduct permutation-based placebo tests in which reform shocks are randomly reassigned across country-year observations and the local projections are re-estimated. The exercise can be interpreted as a Monte Carlo permutation test: rather than drawing artificial shocks from a parametric distribution, we permute the observed reform shocks in order to preserve the empirical distribution of our reform measures. This is important because pension reforms are discrete, infrequent, and unevenly distributed across countries and years, and are therefore not well approximated by standard parametric distributions. The procedure breaks the link between the actual timing of reforms and subsequent macroeconomic outcomes, while keeping the distribution of reform shocks unchanged. For each horizon, we provide ridgeline plots reporting the empirical distribution of impulse responses obtained from 1000 permutations. If the baseline estimates reflect the actual timing of pension reforms rather than a mechanical feature of the estimation procedure, randomly reassigned reform shocks should not generate systematic response patterns.

The resulting placebo distributions are reported in Appendix Figure 1. Overall, the distributions appear centered around zero and do not display systematic dynamic patterns across horizons. This supports the interpretation that the baseline results are not driven mechanically by the estimation procedure or by the unconditional distribution of reform shocks.

Additional control for fiscal adjustments. We do control for business cycles at various stages of our empirical exercise: firstly, in the conditional factor analysis, by adjusting variables for GDP growth ; secondly, by including unemployment rate and a crisis dummy in the set of regressors in the local projections. However, in order to be sure our estimates do not confound pension reforms with coinciding fiscal consolidations, we include, as an additional precaution, explicit measures of fiscal consolidations based on the narrative dataset by Guajardo, Leigh, & Pescatori (2014).

More specifically, our baseline LP specification is extended to include, contemporaneously and with up to three lags, three alternative measures of fiscal consolidation: (i) the overall size of the fiscal consolidation, (ii) the associated spending cuts, and (iii) the corresponding tax increases. Despite the loss of observations due to the more limited time coverage of these measures –up to 2019–, results reported on Appendix Figure 2 remain highly consistent with our previous findings, qualitatively identical and quantitatively very close.

Spillovers and external pressure. Our specifications include country fixed effects and year dummies. While the latter capture common dynamics across countries, they do not account for the possibility that exogenous foreign developments affect country-specific dynamics. For instance, pension reforms enacted abroad may raise expectations of similar reforms at home, with macroeconomic effects that would then be wrongly attributed to domestic dynamics.

To control for such spillovers and this “external reform pressure”, we augment the baseline LP specification with the leave-one-out means of our age and funded-pension reform measures, as well as the leave-one-out mean of an indicator for reform-voting years, both contemporaneously and with up to three lags. Results, reported in Appendix Figure 3, are virtually indistinguishable from the baseline.

Uncertainty. In a similar vein, pension reforms are often hotly debated and sometimes trigger social unrest, which may disrupt the implementation of the reforms as initially planned. The resulting uncertainty may significantly affect our macroeconomic outcome variables. We therefore augment the baseline LP specification with controls for uncertainty based on Google Trends data, which are only available from 2004 onwards. Specifically, we include, both contemporaneously and with up to three lags, the domestic Google Trends index (as a measure of domestic uncertainty) and its leave-one-out mean (as a measure of foreign uncertainty).

Results are reported in Appendix Figure 4. They are fairly noisy, owing to the smaller post-2004 sample. Nonetheless, they are qualitatively close to the baseline, with no systematic difference in the direction of the responses.

7 Conclusion

Population ageing places advanced economies under increasing pressure to reform their pension systems. Yet pension reforms are not homogeneous policy shocks. They differ in the instruments they use, in the timing of their implementation, and in the macroeconomic channels through which they operate. This paper has studied the dynamic macroeconomic effects of pension reforms by combining a new narrative database of major pension reforms in 17 OECD countries over the period 1980-2025 with a conditional factor-analysis approach and local projections.

Our first contribution is to construct reform measures that capture not only the occurrence of pension reforms but also their magnitude and gradual implementation path, going beyond standard dummy-based approaches. Our second contribution is to summarise the multidimensional structure of pension reforms into two orthogonal dimensions: the Age factor, which captures increases in statutory or early-retirement ages, and the Capitalisation factor, which is related to shifts toward funded private pension schemes. Because the latter is identified from a smaller and more geographically concentrated set of reform episodes, the main analysis focuses on the Age factor, while results for the Capitalisation factor are interpreted as complementary and more suggestive evidence.

The main results show that reforms delaying retirement generate a broad expansionary response. They raise the labour force participation rate of workers aged 55-64 and increase aggregate labour force participation. They also increase real GDP and potential GDP, suggesting that the output gains are not merely cyclical but reflect an expansion of productive capacity. Consumption and investment rise in levels, and investment also increases as a share of GDP. On the fiscal side, public pension expenditure declines as a share of GDP and government debt ratios fall persistently. These results suggest that retirement-age reforms should not be interpreted as standard fiscal retrenchment shocks. Rather, they operate as positive labour-supply shocks that also generate demand effects through higher labour income .

The complementary results on the Capitalisation factor point to a different pattern, but should be interpreted more cautiously. In our sample, the Capitalisation factor is associated with declines in GDP, consumption, investment, and GDP per worker over the ten-year horizon considered. Although public pension expenditure falls in levels, debt ratios increase, consistent with transition costs and the adverse denominator effect of lower GDP. We do not find evidence, within this horizon, that the Capitalisation factor is associated with a rise in aggregate saving or investment. Instead, the results are more consistent with a demand-compression channel and fiscal transition costs that may outweigh any positive capital-accumulation effect in the medium run. In this regard, we find that the negative responses are concentrated in observations with higher foreign asset holdings relative to domestic savings, a pattern consistent with a possible role for savings outflows.

The main findings on retirement-age reforms are robust to various sensitivity checks. The results have two broader implications. First, the macroeconomic effects of pension reforms depend crucially on the instrument used. Treating all pension retrenchments as equivalent fiscal consolidation measures risks obscuring important differences between reforms that expand labour supply and reforms that alter pension financing arrangements. Second, the design and timing of reforms matter. Retirement-age reforms can improve both growth and fiscal sustainability when the labour-supply and labour-income channels dominate anticipation and adjustment effects. The results on capitalisation reforms suggest that shifts toward funded schemes may entail transition costs and contractionary demand effects, especially if higher private pension contributions do not translate into higher national saving and productive investment.

Several caveats are warranted. Our results may depend on country-specific features — labour-market institutions, pension-system credibility, financial-market depth — and the evidence on capitalisation reforms rests on a more limited set of reform episodes. The ten-year horizon may also be insufficient to capture the full effects of funded schemes on capital accumulation. Future research could examine heterogeneity across institutional settings and assess whether capitalisation reforms deliver different outcomes over longer horizons or under deeper financial markets.

Overall, the paper shows that pension reforms have macroeconomic effects that go well beyond their direct impact on pension expenditure. The main evidence indicates that delaying retirement can simultaneously support output, investment, and fiscal sustainability by expanding labour supply and sustaining labour income. Complementary evidence for the Capitalisation factor suggests that a greater reliance on funded private pensions does not necessarily deliver the expected macroeconomic gains within the horizon studied here. The choice of pension reform instrument is therefore central to understanding the macroeconomic consequences of ageing and the policy trade-offs involved in restoring pension-system sustainability.

BibTeX citation:
@article{blomme2026,
  author = {Blomme, Océane and Grekou, Carl and Grjebine, Thomas and
    Héricourt, Jérôme},
  title = {The {Macroeconomic} {Effects} of {Pension} {Reforms}},
  journal = {Institut français d’économie working paper},
  date = {2026-11-18},
  url = {},
  langid = {en},
  abstract = {This paper studies the macroeconomic effects of pension
    reforms in advanced economies. We build a new narrative database of
    major pension reforms in 17 OECD countries over 1980-2025, recording
    their timing, magnitude, and phase-in across retirement ages,
    early-retirement rules, contribution requirements, and private
    pillars. A conditional factor analysis extracts two orthogonal
    reform dimensions: an *Age* factor (delayed retirement) and a
    *Capitalisation* factor (a financing-related dimension associated
    with funded schemes). Local projections show that retirement-age
    reforms are broadly expansionary: they raise older workers’
    participation, actual and potential GDP, consumption, and
    investment, while lowering pension expenditure and public debt
    ratios. They act as positive labour-supply shocks rather than fiscal
    retrenchments. By contrast, based on fewer episodes, we find
    suggestive evidence that the *Capitalisation* factor is associated
    with persistent declines in GDP, consumption, investment, GDP per
    worker, and higher debt ratios, consistent with transition costs and
    demand compression outweighing capital-accumulation effects over the
    medium run. Overall, the instrument matters: delaying retirement can
    improve both growth and fiscal sustainability, whereas shifting to
    funded schemes does not appear to deliver macroeconomic gains within
    ten years.}
}
